question: What practical advice does Tamar Yehoshua give managers choosing where to work, beyond chasing a top brand or financial upside?

S1.title: Lessons in product leadership and AI strategy from Glean, Google, Amazon, and Slack | Tamar Yehoshua
S1.text:
They're currently the gravity in the space and everyone awesome is going there. And you have to, as a company, know you're one of those companies or you're the opposite. You're losing all the people and they're all going to this other company. I guess any thoughts on that?

Tamar Yehoshua (00:22:43):
Yeah. And it's really bad when you don't have a gravitational pull. It's super hard. I would say that one thing that if you're a manager, I always advise managers, go somewhere where you can recruit. I got a piece of advice from a friend that I thought was amazing advice as a leader. She said to me, "Take a job where if you hire people, it's going to make their careers." I was like, "Whoa." Because I was getting offers for some turnaround jobs. And if you think you can turn around, great. But if you're going to hire the best people, you want to make sure that it's going to be a good place for them and that they're going to learn and they're going to grow. And so you want to do right by them. And you really earnestly want to say you can make your career by coming here.

answer.summary: Yehoshua advises managers to choose a place where they can recruit people into work that will help those people learn and advance. Evaluate the actual team and working environment—not just the brand or promised financial upside—and prioritize durable skills and personal fit.

sections.heading: Choose a place that is good for the people you hire
sections.content: As a manager, go somewhere you can recruit. Use this test: if you hire people there, will joining make their careers? Make sure they can learn and grow, and that you can earnestly tell candidates the job can help advance their careers. This is a higher bar than simply taking a turnaround role because you think you might fix it.

sections.heading: Prioritize learning over brand or predicted payout
sections.content: You do not have to work at a top-brand company; there are many good companies and paths. Choose somewhere you expect to learn: even if the company fails, the learning and skills remain. Yehoshua says financial success is especially hard to predict because markets and world events can change; she considers taking a job just because it pays a lot a dangerous bet, and recalls that it did not work out for one person.

sections.heading: Check the partners, alignment, and fit
sections.content: Before joining, assess whether you have a good engineering partner who can help get ideas built. Clarify roles, responsibilities, and where you will collaborate versus divide work, so people do not receive conflicting direction. Also consider whether the company’s way of operating fits you: some chaos may be acceptable, but constant changes to strategy, direction, or projects that prevent people from achieving anything are a warning. A successful company may still be a poor personal fit.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately captures Yehoshua’s advice to choose a workplace where hires can learn, grow, and advance their careers, and to favor learning and durable skills over prestige or hard-to-predict financial returns. Its additional points about fit and engineering partnership are supported by the cited context.
